Lesson 23: At a Glance

If we take the narrations which state that the first eighty-odd verses of this surah were revealed on the occasion when the delegation of Najran came to debate with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a delegation made up of Christians who wished to discuss with the Prophet (ﷺ) the matter of Jesus (peace be upon him), then all the verses of this lesson would in effect be regarded as revealed on that occasion. But these very narrations themselves make clear that this delegation came in the year 9 AH, known as the Year of Delegations (ʿĀm al-Wufūd), when the fame of Islam's ascendancy had spread throughout the Arabian Peninsula and the surrounding regions, and delegations from various parts of the Arabian Peninsula were arriving in succession to meet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Some of these delegations came to gain information, and some came to propose agreements with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the new circumstances.

As I have said earlier, both the subjects discussed in these verses and the manner in which they are discussed show that these verses were revealed in the period shortly after the Hijrah. This surah contains mostly doctrinal debate with the People of the Book. There are responses to the doubts that arose among the Muslims because of their false beliefs; or responses to the objections they raised concerning the truth of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) prophethood; or the guidance that was revealed concerning the reality of tawhid and shirk in relation to the People of the Book; or the warning that Allah gave here against the conspiracies of the People of the Book, saying that you should not be deceived by them and should remain firm upon your position. Because of these subjects and discussions, my inclination is that these verses are not specific to the delegation of Najran. For this delegation came in 9 AH, whereas for the revelation of these verses there were conditions in Madinah even before 9 AH, so that they were revealed in those conditions, or the whole surah was revealed in them. Therefore, in explaining these verses, we will not keep only the incident of Najran in view, but the address of this surah will be understood as addressed to the People of the Book in general, because according to historical evidence this incident is very late.

As we said above in the introduction, these verses mention the real conflict that was then taking place between the Islamic movement with its beliefs and ideologies, and the People of the Book and the polytheists with their beliefs and ideologies. This battle began with the appearance of Islam and had no pause; especially at that time the conflict became much more intense when the headquarters of the Islamic movement moved to Madinah and an Islamic state was established there. In this ideological battle the polytheists and the Jews were fighting shoulder to shoulder, and the Qur'an records their joint campaign in detail.

It is not improbable that among the Christians living in the surroundings of the Arabian Peninsula, their religious leaders also took part in this ideological battle in some form, and it is also not unlikely that the Christians came to know of the correct beliefs and ideas regarding Jesus (peace be upon him) which the Qur'an had presented, and came to debate this subject with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because the Christians had strayed from their original path concerning Jesus (peace be upon him), and the Qur'an had already criticized this subject and a refutation of the Christians had come with regard to the belief in tawhid.

In this lesson, at the very beginning, the tawhid belief of Islam is presented, purified of the deviations and doubts of the people of shirk, and it is declared that the Qur'an is a criterion (Furqan) between truth and falsehood, and whoever denies the signs of Allah will be regarded as a disbeliever, whether he is from the People of the Book or not. In these verses, with reference to the Qur'an, the attitude of Muslims and believers toward these verses is described, what their attitude toward their Lord should be, and it is clearly stated what the signs of faith are; they are so clear that there is no error in recognizing the believers. And there are also signs of disbelief, and there can be no error in recognizing the disbelievers. He says:

"Allah, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of the system of the universe, there is truly no god except Him. He has sent down to you the Book, bringing the truth, confirming what came before it. Before this He had sent down the Torah and the Gospel as guidance for mankind, and He has sent down the criterion. Indeed, those who reject the signs of Allah will surely face severe punishment." Allah is Almighty, and the Avenger of wrongdoing; nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah. It is He who shapes you in the wombs of your mothers as He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise. It is Allah who has sent this Book down to you. In this Book there are two kinds of verses: the muhkamat, which are the foundations of the Book, and the mutashabihat. Those in whose hearts is deviation always follow the mutashabihat, seeking discord and seeking to give them meanings, while none knows their true meaning except Allah. But those firm in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord," and only people of understanding take heed. (3:1–8)

"Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and those possessed of knowledge; He upholds justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise. Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam. Those who were given the Book differed only after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. And whoever rejects the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning." 

In this lesson there is a threat in which the address is directed to the Jews, for example: "Those who reject the signs of Allah, who unjustly kill the prophets, and kill those who enjoin justice, give them the good news of a painful punishment." When the mention of the killing of prophets comes, the mind goes to the Jews, because it was they who continually carried out this deed. In another verse it comes: "Let not the believers take disbelievers as allies instead of believers." Although the word disbelievers occurs in this verse, it probably refers to the Jews, though it may also include polytheists. Therefore, up to this period of the Islamic movement, some Muslims had maintained relations with their disbelieving polytheist relatives and with their friends among the Jews. So here they were now forbidden from continuing such relations, and were warned about the evil consequences of these relations in such severe words, whether these friends were Jews or polytheists, because for all of them the word "the disbelievers" is used.

Similarly, another verse: "Say to those who disbelieve: you will soon be overcome and gathered into Hell, a dreadful resting place. There is a sign for you in the two groups that met in battle: one fighting in the way of Allah, and the other disbelieving; they saw them with their own eyes, twice their number." This verse refers to the events of the Battle of Badr, but the address is to the Jews. In this regard a narration is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), who said that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) defeated the Quraysh on the day of Badr and returned to Madinah, he gathered the Jews and advised them that they should become Muslims before they meet the same fate as the Quraysh. They said: "Muhammad, indeed you have killed some men of the Quraysh, but do not be deceived by that, for they were inexperienced and did not know much about war. If you fight us, you will know that we are a people, and perhaps you have never encountered people like us." Concerning them Allah revealed this verse: "Say to those who disbelieve: you will soon be overcome, and gathered into Hell..." up to the words "one group fights in the way of Allah," meaning at Badr, and "the other is a disbeliever." (Abu Dawud)

Thus in the verse of this lesson: "Now if they dispute with you, say: I have submitted myself to Allah, and so have those who follow me. And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered: Have you submitted? If they submit, they are rightly guided; and if they turn away, your duty is only to convey the message. Allah is ever watchful over His servants." (3:20) The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and although this address is at the beginning of this lesson of ideological debate with the People of the Book, it is general, and whether the opponents are People of the Book or not. The last part of this verse, "if they turn away, your duty is only to convey the message," shows that at that time jihad against the People of the Book had not yet been made obligatory upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and he did not take jizyah from them. This shows that our view is correct, that the verses under discussion in this lesson were revealed in the early period after the Hijrah.

In sum, by reflecting well upon all these verses, it becomes clear that their connection is not with any single event, such as the arrival of the delegation of Najran; the guidance given in them is general and applies to all opponents of Islam. Yes, among the occasions in relation to which these verses were revealed, the delegation of Najran could be one, because in those early days such occasions occurred repeatedly, since at that time in the Arabian Peninsula there was an all-encompassing ideological battle between the Muslims and their opponents, especially with the Jews of Madinah.

In this first lesson, very important fundamental concepts about the Islamic worldview have been presented. Important clarifications have also been given about the nature and temperament of this way of life. It has also been shown what practical effects this way of life has on human life, and what effects are inseparable from faith, such as regarding Allah as One without partner; and its necessary consequence is that a monotheist also becomes a Muslim to Allah; this is the religion, and there is no other religion. And to be a Muslim means that a person submits himself before Allah and obeys Him: he accepts His commands, accepts His Shariah, and follows His Messenger and the way of life of the Messenger. Thus according to this worldview, if someone does not submit, does not obey, and does not follow the Messenger, he is not a Muslim, and therefore he is not a religious person whose religion Allah has chosen. And Allah has chosen only Islam, and Islam, as we have explained above, is the name of complete submission, obedience and following. This is why the Qur'an comments with great astonishment on the People of the Book when they are invited to judge by the Book of Allah: "a party of them turn away, and they are averse" (3:23). Clearly, in the terminology of the Qur'an this turning away is equivalent to disbelief, and by this turning away their claim of faith is exposed and faith is negated. This truth is further clarified in the second part of this surah... After this brief introduction, it is now appropriate to present the detailed explanation and commentary of the verses of this lesson.

These are the disjointed letters (ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt). An exact explanation of them is not possible, but on a preferred basis I state the meaning I stated at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah: namely, that it points to the challenge that this Book is composed of those very letters which are within the reach of the opponents of Islam, yet despite this the Book is a miracle, and the opponents have failed to bring a book like it.

In the interpretation of these letters which we have preferred, the explanation or indication of this challenge is found in several surahs, including in the very surah in whose beginning these letters occur. For example, in Surah al-Baqarah this indication exists as an explicit challenge:

"And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call your witnesses besides Allah, if you are truthful." (2:23)

In the Surah Āl ʿImrān under discussion, the indication of challenge and defiance is made from another aspect: that this Book has been sent down by Allah, besides whom there is no other god, and it is composed of the same letters and words from which all the other heavenly books were revealed, and in which the People of the Book themselves have already believed, and to whom the greater part of this surah is addressed. Therefore it is no matter of wonder or denial that Allah should send down upon His Messenger a new Book composed of these same letters.

Thus the opening of this surah begins with criticism of the People of the Book who rejected Islam and denied the Messengership of the Prophet (ﷺ). Yet, on the basis of their own religion, and as People of the Book, they were familiar with the concepts of prophethood, messengership, the divine scriptures and revelation. It was therefore their duty to be the first to embrace Islam and to confirm the Messenger (ﷺ), provided that their confirmation depended only on the satisfaction of proof and argument.

In this decisive attack, all the doubts that lay in the hearts of the People of the Book, or that they deliberately sought to plant in the hearts of the believers, and therefore spread as propaganda, were uprooted. In this criticism, the paths and doors through which these doubts entered have been identified. Here, as a preventive measure, it has been made clear what the stance of the true believers is regarding the signs of Allah, and what the thinking of the opponents and deviants is about them. At the beginning of this surah, a beautiful portrayal is given of the true believers' relationship with Allah, their humility before Allah's court, and their supplications. It is also stated that they hold a particular concept of Allah's attributes: ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ (2:255). "Allah is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, who sustains the order of the universe."

This pure and clear Tawhid (the oneness of Allah) in fact draws a line of distinction between the belief of a Muslim and the beliefs of all non-Muslims, including atheists and polytheists, and deviant People of the Book, whether Jews or Christians, according to the differences in their ideas and beliefs. In short, Tawhid is the line of distinction between the beliefs of a Muslim and those of all non-Muslims, because here the system of life is determined by one's worldview and beliefs. It is this belief that determines the system of life.

There is no god but Allah; there is no partner with Him in divinity. He is living, and life is His essential attribute. He is free from every limitation, He is absolutely living. He is al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer); this universe is held by Him alone. Life subsists through Him, and every existing thing exists through Him. Then He keeps everything in existence. Therefore, without Him, no being can continue to exist in the universe, nor can any being come into existence.

This is the line of distinction between a worldview and belief, and this is the difference between the conduct and system of life of a Muslim as compared with a non-Muslim. Through this, the Islamic concept of Tawhid regarding the Being of Allah, and Islamic beliefs, are also distinguished from false beliefs and the darkness of the beliefs of ignorance (Jahiliyyah). The concepts of ignorance include the concepts of the polytheists of Arabia at that time, as well as the deviated concepts of the Jews and Christians which they held.

The Qur'an has recorded, regarding the Jews, that they gave the status of "son of Allah" to Hadrat Uzair (peace be upon him). The false belief mentioned by the Qur'an in the Jewish scripture that they hold sacred is present today in it; for example, in the Book of Genesis, chapter six, there is mention:

"When men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born to them, the 'sons' of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful; and they took wives for themselves of all that they chose. Then the LORD said, My Spirit shall not strive with man forever, for he is indeed flesh; yet his days shall be one hundred and twenty years. There were giants on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men and they bore children to them. Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown."

Regarding the corruptions that arose in Christian concepts, the Qur'an has related their saying: ﴿Allah is the third of three﴾ (5:73), and their saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary﴾ (5:72). It is also stated that they had taken Hadrat Messiah and his mother as two gods besides Allah, and that they had taken their rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah. The famous author Arnold writes in his book "The Preaching of Islam":

"About one hundred years before the rise of Islam, Emperor Justinian had apparently succeeded in creating unity in the Roman Empire, but after his death the empire fell into pieces, because a common feeling of nationality no longer remained between the capital and the provinces. Heraclius tried to reattach the land of Syria to the central government, and he did have some success in this, but unfortunately the methods of reconciliation he adopted increased the disagreement rather than removing it. In people's hearts, religious prejudices had taken the place of national feeling. Therefore the Emperor tried to interpret and explain the Christian religion in such a way that the mutual disputes of the opposing sects would disappear, and that those who had deviated from the religion would be united with the Orthodox Church and the central government. At the council of Chalcedon, which sat in 451 AD, the assembly of Christian scholars declared the belief that "two natures (hypostases) of Hadrat Jesus (peace be upon him) must be accepted, in such a way that there is no mixing, change, division or separation between them. The difference of their natures, which is not nullified by their union, but the properties of each hypostasis remain, and they exist in one person and one being. But not in such a way that these properties are divided or separated between two beings, but rather he is the one Son, the only-begotten, the Word of God." However, the Monophysite sect rejected this belief, because those people held that "in the person of the Messiah there is only one hypostasis; this person is a composite in which all divine and human attributes are included. But the being in which these attributes are present is not dual, but is a composite unity." The people of this sect lived especially in Syria, Egypt, and the lands outside the Roman Empire. Thus the debate on this issue between these two sects continued heatedly for two centuries, until Heraclius came and sought to create reconciliation between the parties through the doctrine of Monothelitism. The meaning of this belief was that, while accepting the duality of hypostases, the unity of the person in the actual life of the Messiah should be maintained, because two streams of will and action cannot be accepted in one single person. Thus the Messiah, who is the Son of God, produces both human and divine results through one single means and channel, that is, in the incarnate Word there is only one will at work."

"But the fate of Heraclius was the same as that of many who try to make peace, because not only did the fire of controversy blaze up even more, but people accused the Emperor of irreligion, and both sects became objects of censure."

Another Christian, Mr. Canon Taylor, writes that at the time of the mission of Hadrat Muhammad (ﷺ), the condition of Eastern Christians was that in reality they were polytheists. They worshipped a class of martyrs. Likewise, Christians worshipped saints and angels, and the least of their polytheistic beliefs was that, according to them, they served these gods only so that through their service they might gain nearness to Allah. ﴿We do not worship them except that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ (39:3).

In this jungle and heap of wrong beliefs and concepts, to which we have already alluded, Islam came and gave the decisive, explicit and clearly distinguished concept of the Islamic worldview and the Islamic creed: ﴿There is no god but Allah; He is the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ (2:255). This belief and this concept of life was such that it separated the paths of the two parties; it divided their conduct and their way of life... The person in whose thought and consciousness it is that Allah is one, without partner, and that there is no god but Him, that He is living and that in this sense there is no other living being, and that the existence of all other beings subsists with Him, and that He is the one who sustains all beings and all living things, ... the person who holds this belief and these attributes must certainly have a system of life and a way of living different from the person whose mental world is covered with clouds of false and superstitious concepts, of which we have spoken above. The effects that can be produced on the life of a person who holds such false concepts cannot be the same as those produced on the life of one who believes in a God who is active and dispossessing in his life and is powerful over all things.

It is only the blessing of pure Tawhid that, as a result, a human being can worship only one god. In such a concept, a person does not seek help from anyone other than Allah. He seeks victory only from Allah. He does not take his system of life or his system of law from anyone other than Allah, nor does he take morals and manners from anyone other than Allah. Nor does he take social and economic systems from strangers. In short, a monotheist does not take anything from other than Allah in any field of his life, nor does he give importance to anyone other than Allah in his concept of the life after death. As for those crooked, deviant, complex, polytheistic ignorant beliefs, their adherents have no fixed direction, nor do these beliefs have stability; nor do they have the limits of the lawful and unlawful; nor is there any distinction in them between right and wrong; neither in system and law, nor in manners and morals, nor in conduct and behaviour. In short, all these matters are settled only when the direction of them is determined in a person's belief and worldview. After that, a person turns towards that source and that direction and worships and obeys it.

And when Islam established that ﴿Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾, then a Muslim turned to Allah alone, and thus his path and the paths of those of other beliefs became separate.

It is for this reason that, because of this doctrinal separation, the temperament of the Islamic system of life has become entirely distinct. Islamic life, with all its constituent elements, is wholly shaped by the Islamic worldview. And the Islamic worldview is based on pure and complete Tawhid, and this belief of Tawhid does not settle permanently in the human conscience until some practical effects of it are produced in life, for example, in every field of life, alongside the belief in Tawhid, a person also takes the human system of law from Allah, and turns towards the Divine Being in every activity and endeavour of life.

After the explanation of pure Tawhid, a comprehensive Tawhid in which there is no partner in His Being and no partner in His attributes, now comes the explanation of the source and origin from which a Muslim takes his religion: the place from which divine scriptures and the teachings of the Messengers are sent down, that is, the place from which, in every age and every era, human beings have derived their systems of life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 3, verses 3–4:

The first sentence of this verse mentions all the fundamental truths of the Islamic conception of life. Among the People of the Book and others, those who denied the prophethood of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) are refuted, and what Allah has sent down is affirmed as true.

This verse shows that guidance descends only from Allah. All the heavenly books are from Him. Allah is the one besides whom there is no deity (ilah), He is the Ever-Living (al-Hayy), the Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyum). It is He who sent down this Quran upon you, and it is He who sent down the Torah upon Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) before it, and it is He who sent down the Injil upon Hazrat Isa (peace be upon him). Therefore, in His divinity and in worship of Him, there is no partnership or admixture with anyone else. He alone is the deity who sends down books upon His chosen servants, and those servants receive guidance from Him. And those who receive it are also servants of Allah, even if they are prophets.

This verse shows that the path of guidance in the heavenly books is one religion, because the truth that this book has brought to you confirms all the truths that were revealed to the earlier prophets, such as the Torah and the Injil. The aim of all these books and messengerships has been one and the same, namely to bring people onto the straight path. Then, this book that has been sent down upon you has another attribute: since the followers of the heavenly books have made many distortions (tahrif) in them over the passage of time, it is also the Furqan (the criterion that distinguishes truth from falsehood). It distinguishes between the original guidance of those heavenly books and the distorted guidance, and it shows what is the original, and what is deviation and what is distortion, as we gave an example of this in the lengthy excerpt from Arnold's book "The Preaching of Islam".

Incidentally, this also settles that the People of the Book have no justification for denying this new messengership, because the path of this messengership is the same path on which the earlier messengerships stood. This book was sent down in the same way as the books before it were sent down. Just as earlier books were sent down upon a human messenger, so too this book has been sent down upon a human being. This book confirms all the earlier books and messengers. Just as it is based on truth, so too those books were based on truth. And this book was sent down by the One who has the right to send down truth, because only He has the authority to prescribe a system of life for human beings, to set out their intellectual concepts for them, to prescribe a Shariah for them, and to prescribe a system of morals and etiquette for them; and all these books are present within this Book of Revelation.

The second part of this verse contains a terrifying warning for those who deny the signs of Allah without any proof. It is stated that Allah is Mighty (Aziz), He is the possessor of overwhelming powers, His seizing is severe, and He sometimes also takes revenge, which is very terrifying. Those who deny the signs of Allah are, in effect, denying all the religions which are one in their origin. The People of the Book first denied this book which was sent down upon them, and whose text they distorted; now they deny this book. Because they had also distorted their own books, this new book is a Furqan for them. Therefore this severe threat is addressed to them, and they are told: beware of the revenge of Allah.

Following the threat of punishment and divine retribution, they are also told that nothing about anyone is hidden from the being of Allah. Nothing is concealed from Him, and nothing can escape Him.

إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَخْفَى عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ فِي الأرْضِ وَلا فِي السَّمَاءِ
﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah.﴾

Allah is the Being to whom nothing existing within the earth and the heavens is concealed. That nothing is hidden from Him, and that He knows everything, is because He is the Deity (al-Ilah), He is the One who sustains this universe. Therefore His knowledge encompasses all things. The attribute of al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer) is mentioned at the beginning of the surah. Moreover, the attribute of the all-encompassing knowledge is mentioned here specifically because this verse also carries a frightening warning. The meaning is that it is impossible for anything to be kept hidden from Him. Nothing in the earth and the heavens is concealed from Him. No intention or purpose can be hidden from Him. No plan is hidden from Him. In the same way, within His system it is impossible for anyone to escape punishment or to remain beyond the reach of His knowledge.

Under the shadow of this subtle and precise knowledge of Allah, the human consciousness is given a jolt concerning its own creation. This nudge is given to human consciousness regarding the very creation of man: the creation of man, which takes place in the realm of the unseen, in the hidden darkness of the womb, a process about which man's knowledge has been unable to reach, nor does he comprehend it, and that process has not come within the sphere of human power to create.

He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise. (Qur'an 3:6, in this passage's rendering of the verse's meaning)

Note: the quoted verse fragments above are not my own addition; here is the full translation of the passage as requested:

He shapes you in the wombs in whatever form He wills. Then He also bestows upon you the characteristics appropriate to that form and shape. There is no god but Allah, for no other being shares in this act of fashioning; He does it solely by His own will and His own purpose, "as He wills." "There is no god but He." "He is the Mighty." "He has complete power over this creation and fashioning." "He is the Wise"; this whole process of creation is founded upon a very profound technology. No obstacle comes in its way, and no one has any share with Him in this work.

The purpose of pointing to the creation of man here is that the address is directed to the People of the Book, and among the People of the Book there were extremely wrong notions and doubts regarding the creation of Hadrat Isa (peace be upon him). It is Allah who fashioned Hadrat Isa as He willed. The belief that Hadrat Isa is himself a lord, or is God, or is the son of God, or is some divine-human hypostasis (aqnum) of the Lahut and Nasut, is false. This is because these concepts, besides being incomprehensible and beyond grasp, also contradict the correct, intelligible and clear concept of the doctrine of Tawhid.

After this, the Qur'an identifies those whose hearts have deviation in them. These are the people who, leaving aside the decisive (muhkam) verses of the Qur'an, pursue those verses whose meaning admits of interpretation, so that by giving false interpretations of such verses they may create doubts about Islamic beliefs. This identification is made so that the true characteristics of the people of faith and of the people of realities may be stated: that it be explained how pure their faith is, and how they act upon Allah's definitive commands without any questioning or hesitation. They say:

A narration reports that the Christian delegation of Najran asked the Messenger (ﷺ), "Do you believe that Jesus is the Word of Allah (Kalimatullah) and the Spirit of Allah (Ruhullah)?" They wanted to use these words to establish their false beliefs about 'Isa (peace be upon him). For example, they claimed that he was not a human being but the Spirit of Allah, and they interpreted the "Spirit of Allah" in their own way. Yet they never spoke of those Qur'anic verses on this subject that were definitive (muhkamat, the clear and decisive verses), which affirmed the absolute oneness of Allah and categorically denied that Allah has any partner or any son. Therefore Allah revealed those verses and exposed their scheme, by which they exploited the ambiguous expressions (mutashabihat) of the Qur'an and ignored the verses that are definitive in meaning.

However, this statement is general in its meaning. It comments on the varying positions that people of different schools of thought have taken regarding the verses of the Qur'an. It is thus made clear that the Qur'an is a book of guidance. Some of its matters relate to the foundations of faith and the fundamental truths of Islamic thought. Some contain the details of the Islamic system of life, and some verses describe unseen matters, the true concept of which lies beyond the range of our limited reason, and which human perception cannot grasp with its present limited means of knowledge. Most of these texts describe matters that lie beyond human perception.

The Qur'an revealed definitive verses concerning the first two matters, namely belief and the concepts and ideas of the worldview, and the Islamic system of life and Shari'ah. These can be conceived, and their purposes are entirely clear, and these two fields are the main subject of the Qur'an. As for those matters about which the Messenger (ﷺ) gave information, or which the Qur'an reported and which we have recited and taught, the unseen reports that the Qur'an relates, including the report of the birth of the Messiah, the guidance concerning them is this: to the extent that you can understand them, you should certainly extend your understanding, but beyond the limit of comprehension, believe that these are a true matter from the Real Creator, and that their reality and mode are at present difficult to grasp, because by their very nature they lie beyond humanity's present means.

As for those people, they consider these verses through the lens of their own personalities. If they are sound in thought, their understanding is sound; if their thinking is crooked, their understanding is also crooked. Because of their crooked nature they have gone astray, and such people ignore the clear and plain verses of the Qur'an. They abandon the evident principles, which are most detailed, and on which the Islamic view of life and the Islamic system of living are founded. These people pursue the mutashabihat, whose verification depends solely on faith and on the fact that they were revealed by Allah.

Their correct meanings are known to Allah alone, since human means of knowledge are relative and the field of their perceptive power is limited. Moreover, their correct understanding depends on the direct inspiration and awareness which a sound-minded person receives regarding the truth of the Book of Allah, that this entire Book is a true Book, that it was revealed with truth, and that falsehood can attack it in no respect. Those with crooked hearts and minds pursue these mutashabihat because they find in these verses opportunities through which they create turmoil, and they devise interpretations by which doubts can be introduced into the Islamic concept of life. When they have created intellectual confusion through these, they then bring that confusion into verses that are entirely definitive and clear. Yet the interpretation of the mutashabihat is known to Allah alone: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah.﴾

As for those who are firm in knowledge, those who have, by means of knowledge, understood that human reason, human thought, and this reason and thought, with their present power and present means of reason and thought, cannot attain the meanings of these mutashabihat, they say with full conviction and tranquillity: ﴿We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.﴾ This faith leads them to the conclusion, with great certainty, that these verses are from Allah, and therefore they are true and founded on truth. What Allah has decided is in itself true, and it is neither part of the duty of human reason nor within its power to investigate the causes and reasons of these verses, to discover the nature of their meanings, or to search out the causes and reasons hidden within them. When these verses are presented before those who are firm in knowledge, they accept their truth. Through their truthful nature and far-reaching understanding they are satisfied, and their reason does not doubt them at all. This is because they have grasped that knowledge and wisdom consist in not being interested in a reality whose comprehension is not possible through knowledge and reason, especially those matters that lie beyond the limits of human means of knowledge.

This is an excellent portrayal of ﴿those firm in knowledge﴾, and only a superficial person can deny this portrayal and praise. Because of their shallow knowledge, such people fall into the delusion that they have acquired everything, and that whatever is not within their knowledge does not exist. They assume that they have grasped everything, so the form of all realities is whatever comes to their minds. By this they measure the absolute and unrestricted speech of Allah according to the standards and fortresses of their rationalism, although these standards do not fit within their limited reason. Thus countless realities lie beyond the sphere of human reason. Since such people are naturally inclined to believe, the truth reaches their true nature quickly, they confirm it, and they are satisfied: ﴿And none will be reminded except the people of understanding.﴾

When a person reaches this station of wisdom, his reward comes from Allah. He becomes humble and submissive, and with supplication he prays: O Allah, keep us firm upon the truth, do not let us go astray after having been guided, and pour upon us Your mercy and Your grace. The fear of the Hereafter takes hold of them, for they must surely go to where there is no escape.

Those who are firm in knowledge have a relationship with their Lord, and this is the kind of relationship that a true believer ought to have. It arises from complete reliance upon the word of Allah and His covenant, and it is attained through a correct awareness of Allah's grace and mercy, especially when a believer also holds firm conviction in Allah's decree and destiny (qada wa qadar), and the fear of Allah surges in his heart. A believer is neither heedless, nor arrogant, nor does he ever forget his obligations in his daily life and night.

After the straying and misguidance of the heart, the attainment of the wealth of faith is greatly valued by the believer. After a vague conception, seeing the truth with one's own eyes is of great importance to his heart. After bewilderment and confusion, finding the straight path makes him aware. After doubt and uncertainty, when he finds tranquility, he rejoices greatly; he is freed from all the servitudes of the world and enters into the servitude of the One Allah, and he is delighted, and he is conscious that Allah, the Exalted, has given him much by granting the wealth of faith……………Therefore he fears greatly the path of misguidance again. Since he has already come onto the right path, he greatly dreads being trapped again in the ups and downs and dark paths of misguidance. He fears in the way that a person who sits in pleasant weather under dense shade may fear, even at the thought of the scorching heat and the waterless desert. The truth is that the value of faith and the taste of certainty can only be attained by one who has seen the harsh days of wretchedness and the days of dryness of the mind that come with atheism and godlessness. Only such a person can properly estimate how much sweetness there is in the life of faith compared with the life of irreligion, misguidance, and immorality.

This is why, in such situations, a believer turns to his Lord with such humility and submission. ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us……………﴾ "O our Lord! After showing us the path of guidance, do not make our hearts crooked." They supplicate that, after misguidance, they have received a great mercy, and they fear it might be lost; this is a bounty than which there is no greater bounty.

﴿Grant us mercy from Yourself; indeed You are the Bestower……………﴾ "Grant us mercy from Your treasury of the unseen; You alone are the true Bestower." That is, through their awareness of faith, these people are certain that they can do nothing without the grace and mercy of Allah. Even their hearts are not in their own hands. Therefore they supplicate before Allah for their guidance and for their salvation in the Hereafter.

It is narrated from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) often made this supplication: "All hearts are between two fingers of Ar-Rahman; when He wills to set them straight, He sets them straight, and when He wills to make them crooked, He makes them crooked." And when a believer properly becomes aware of this matter, he clings with great warmth to the threshold of the Divine court, and, beseeching humbly, he asks for Allah's assistance and tawfiq, and turning toward Him, he seeks His mercy and His grace and bounty, so that the treasure He has bestowed upon this believer remains preserved, and the generosity with which he has been favored endures.

After this, the address turns toward the disbelievers. It is told what their end will be and what the sunnah of Allah concerning them is, in which no change ever occurs. The meaning is that their sins will certainly be called to account. Those among the People of the Book who deny this religion and stand blocking its path are warned that they should desist, and through the Messenger (ﷺ) they are admonished to take lesson from the evil end of the disbelievers of Makkah, which took place before their eyes, in which their great army was defeated by a small band.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 3, verse 10:

These verses are addressed to the Children of Israel. In them a warning is given that they should reflect on the end of the disbelievers, both what has already happened and what is yet to come. There is a subtle and profound indication here: Allah destroyed Pharaoh and granted deliverance to the Children of Israel, but that destruction was not because Pharaoh was Pharaoh, but because he was a disbeliever. And the deliverance of the Children of Israel was not because they had a lineal relationship with the people of Israel, but because they were people of faith. Therefore, if they now adopt the path of disbelief and misguidance, they will not deserve deliverance. If they go astray, they will not be able to escape being called people of disbelief. Likewise, they will certainly encounter the evil end of the disbelievers in this world and the Hereafter, just as the people of Pharaoh met that end because of their disbelief.

Similarly, they are directed to the battlefield of Badr, to the fate of the Quraysh. They were struck by that condition solely because they were disbelievers. If they too remain upon disbelief, then the sunnah of Allah is that they will certainly meet the same end that the Quraysh met. This is because the root cause of that end was disbelief. With Allah there is no special treatment for anyone, nor does intercession work there; only sound faith can be an intercessor there.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah in the least; and they are the fuel of the Fire.﴾

In this world wealth and children are a support for protection, but these two things will not avail on that day about whose coming there is no doubt. This is because Allah has promised that day, and there is never any failure in the promise of Allah. The promise of Allah is never postponed; the disbelievers will be the fuel of Hell. The manner of expression used here indicates that the people of Hell will be stripped of human qualities and will be like dry refuse and fuel in the Fire. On that occasion neither wealth and riches, nor status, nor kingdom will be of any use to them.

"Their fate will be just like that of Pharaoh's people and those before them, who denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment."

This is an example that has been repeated many times in history, and Allah has related several of its accounts in His Book with great detail. In those accounts is found Allah's sunnah (established way) concerning those who deny His signs. Wherever Allah wills, He puts this sunnah into action. Therefore, those who deny the signs of Allah have no guarantee in this world, nor are they safe. So those who now reject the Prophethood of Muhammad and deny the Quran that was revealed to him will certainly face this same end, both in this world and in the Hereafter. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is here commanded to warn these disbelievers and People of the Book of this evil end. If they have forgotten the evil end of Pharaoh and the other disobedient nations of Islamic history, then, for God's sake, let the people of Makkah reflect on the evil end that has already been displayed before their very eyes. All of this is nothing but the consequence of denying the signs.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 3, verse 13:

On this verse, ﴿They saw them as twice their number with their own eyes﴾ ……………, there can be two meanings. If the pronoun in "yarawnahum" refers to the disbelievers, and "us" (the pronoun for those who are seen) refers to the believers, the meaning is that the people of disbelief, despite their apparent numerical superiority, were seeing the people of Islam as twice their number. Thus this was a divine support from Allah: the disbelievers saw the people of Islam as more and themselves as few. In this way their feet slipped and their hearts sank.

And if it is taken the other way around, that is, "yarawnahum" means that the Muslims were seeing them, then the meaning is that the disbelievers appeared to the Muslims as twice their own number, when in fact they were three times. Despite this, the people of Islam remained steadfast and were victorious. The fundamental point is that help and victory are in the hand of Allah. Therefore what is desired through this display is that the people of disbelief should reflect upon their end, and that the people of Islam should strengthen their hearts and be certain that defeat has already been written in the destiny of their enemies, so they should not fear those enemies. As we said while commenting on this surah, the situation at that time required this kind of warning and intimidation for the People of the Book.

The Qur'an continuously adheres to its great truth, and one aspect of this great truth is that those who disbelieve in this world, deny the signs and deviate from the Islamic system of life, their defeat is promised and this promise remains in place now and will remain so. Likewise, Allah's promise to the believers also remains in place: that they will be victorious even if they are few in number, and that victory and triumph depend solely on divine support, which is solely in His power; He grants victory to whom He wills. The reality remains as it is now; it has not been abrogated.

It is the duty of the believers to be fully assured of this truth, to place complete trust in it, and to make their preparations for the field of jihad as completely as possible. After that preparation, they should await divine support. They should neither be hasty nor despair, even if they must wait a long time, because Allah is Wise; He carries out His measures Himself at His appointed time, and in accordance with that wisdom His promise is fulfilled at its proper time.

﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those who have vision﴾ ……………. There is a great lesson hidden in this for those who have seeing eyes. Therefore it is necessary to have an observant eye and a discerning insight that plans; only then can a person derive a lesson, and only then does understanding arise in the heart. Without insight, the materials for lessons pass before the eyes day and night, yet the eye does not see.

In the next verse, in the training of the Muslim community, it is made aware of the natural inclinations and natural causes from which deviation and straying begin in a human life. Therefore there is a great need to keep these natural inclinations under constant restraint and control, to always keep the lofty purposes of life in view, and to make the true objective the honour and reward that a person may receive on the Day of Judgement.

The truth is that becoming lost in worldly desires, pursuing the enjoyments of the self, and becoming a slave to other natural inclinations results in the hearts losing insight, and the intellect losing the ability to learn from lessons. A person comes to be compelled by sensory pleasures and worldly enjoyments. Lofty and exalted purposes fade from view. Human feelings become material; he cannot go beyond the circle of the pleasures of this near world, and he is deprived of the delight of achieving those lofty purposes which relate to the human station of being the vicegerent (khalifah) of Allah on earth, and which are befitting of this creature of the world whom Allah has made His khalifah in this vast kingdom, the world.

It is worth noting here that since these natural inclinations and worldly enjoyments are, from Allah, the creational duties of a human being, and since these tendencies play an important role in the growth and development of human life in this world and are a kind of natural obligation, Islam does not indicate the elimination or uprooting of these natural inclinations. Rather, Islam commands that these inclinations be made subject to a discipline: that they be organised, that their intensity be reduced, and that they be controlled in such a way that a person has full mastery over them, that the person is their owner and manager, and that the person keeps his gaze fixed on lofty goals beyond them and considers himself elevated above their slavery.

Therefore the verses of the Qur'an discuss these enjoyments and inclinations. However, in this verse Allah mentions the otherworldly delights, those enjoyments related to food and drink, and those related to intellect and understanding. These otherworldly delights will be the portion of those who exercised control over their souls in this world, who were not drowned in luxury and pleasures in this world, and who kept themselves elevated to the station of humanity here.

In this single verse, the Qur'an, in the course of its discourse, has gathered together all the important desires of this world at once. For example: women, children, wealth and gold, horses and mounts, fertile land and various kinds of livestock. All the desires possible in this world have been gathered in this verse. Either these things are themselves among the desires, or they are a means of acquiring desires for a person. Along with this, another verse mentions the enjoyments and delights which Allah has prepared in this world for the believers, the gardens beneath which rivers flow, pure spouses, and, greater than all these favours, the pleasure and good-pleasure of the Lord. These blessings are only for those whose gaze is higher than these worldly delights and whose connection is with Allah. Now, let us reflect upon these verses.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 3, verse 14:

By using the passive form in "zuyyina lil-nas" (it has been made attractive to people), attention is drawn to the fact that people's inclination towards these things is in accordance with their nature. These things have been made beloved, and by adorning them their beloved status has been increased. In other words, this is a confirmation of one aspect of a factual reality, because inclination and desire for these things has been placed in the personality of a human being. It is part of his original existence and his self. There is no need for a person to needlessly deny this reality, nor should a person himself regard these inclinations and tendencies within his own self as objectionable. For the progress and growth of human life on this earth, the presence of these inclinations is absolutely necessary, as we have already discussed in detail on this subject earlier. But it is also a factual reality that the human nature has another aspect, which creates a balance between these inclinations and natural tendencies, and which acts as a kind of watchman that protects a person from becoming absorbed in these inclinations. This aspect maintains the spiritual connection of a human being with the higher world. Accordingly, spiritual meaning and spiritual guidance are found in his life. This aspect is the spiritual side of a human's life, which creates within him the capacity for elevation. Within him the power of self-restraint comes into being, and as a result a person remains at a moderate limit in the use of these worldly desirable things, within limits in which the self is built, life is nourished, and alongside this the struggle continues to raise human life from the lowest level of animality to the spiritual horizon of the higher world. The heart of a human being remains connected with the higher world, and his aim is the Hereafter and the pleasure of Allah. This second instinct of the human self refines his first natural instinct, and purifies it from all animal admixtures, and confines it within such bounds and restrictions that as a result natural inclinations do not become rebellious, and a person does not become merely a captive of worldly pleasures, such that human spiritual values are suppressed and the paths of God-consciousness, fear of Allah, and the lofty values of life are completely closed.

"Zuyyina lil-nas hubb al-shahawat" (The love of desires has been made attractive to people): these desires are permissible and pleasant... they are not repulsive or filthy. The manner of expression is such that it does not show the filthiness or repulsiveness of these desires. The verse only seeks to explain the nature and reality of these things, and intends to show their effects. Also, what is intended here is to determine the worth and station of these things, so that they cannot go beyond that station, nor can they lay hands on the values which are higher and more exalted in comparison to them. A person should not remain simply immersed in these worldly desires, but his gaze should be constantly fixed on the Hereafter, even though he continues to enjoy these pleasures to the extent of need.

Here it becomes clear that Islam takes human nature as a factual reality and gives due consideration to natural inclinations. It refines, civilises and elevates these inclinations. It never uproots these inclinations in any way. Those who today, in the subject of psychology, speak of the harms of uprooting inclinations, or discuss the psychological complications which arise as a result of the uprooting of emotions, they affirm that psychological complications arise from the suppression of emotions, not from their control and refinement. And uprooting means regarding the demand of nature as filth and considering its commission to be evil. The result of doing so is that an individual comes under the pressure of two different kinds of inclinations from different directions. On one hand, his consciousness and inclination arise from his ideology, his religion, or his customs. For example, his ideology may be that all natural inclinations are wholly filthy, that they should not exist at all, and that in reality they are satanic inclinations. But what happens is that no ideological or religious consciousness has ever succeeded in suppressing these natural tendencies. Therefore these inclinations are natural, and they have deep roots in nature. Moreover, their connection is sometimes with the function of the survival of humanity; without them the duty of the survival of humanity cannot be fulfilled. Allah Ta'ala did not place these inclinations in human nature without purpose. As a result of this conflict, psychological complications arise. Even if we accept these psychological discussions, it will still be seen that Islam long ago created a balance between these two tendencies and inclinations of human nature. By creating a beautiful balance between desires, pleasure, and moral elevation and purity, it has permitted both to function within the bounds of moderation at their own proper station.

"Zuyyina lil-nas hubb al-shahawat min al-nisa' wal-banin wal-qanatir al-muqantara min al-dhahab wal-fiddah wal-khayl al-musawwama wal-an'am wal-harth"

"It has been made attractive to people: the love of desires, women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle and tilled land."

Women and children are among the most powerful and intense desires of human beings. Alongside these, the mention of heaped-up piles of gold and silver is also made. The accumulation of the greatest amount of wealth is expressed by "wal-qanatir al-muqantara". If only the condemnation of wealth and property were intended, the word would have been "min al-amwal", and not "min al-dhahab wal-fiddah"; but the words "qanatir muqantara", meaning heaps of wealth and piles of gold and silver, give a particular shade of meaning, namely that the accumulation of wealth in itself is a desirable thing. As for its benefits, these are known to all; these heaps become the means of supplying every kind of desire for a person. Along with women, children, and heaped gold and silver, here "wal-khayl al-musawwama" (branded horses) is mentioned. Horses, just as in this material and industrial age they are considered a beloved means of transport, were in that age extremely beloved and desirable. This is because they possess beauty and grace, they are full of splendour and swift in movement, and they have intelligence and immense love for their master. Even those people who have never actually ridden horses also enjoy seeing them, as long as they still have enough vitality to be delighted at the sight of a strong and young horse.

After these desires, the mention of other livestock and cultivated land follows. There is an inseparable bond between livestock and cultivated land, which is why they are mentioned together. They are together both in the mind and in factual reality. Livestock, fields, and lush green crops, where the work of growth continues, are desirable pleasures for a human being, because life bursts forth from these fields, and it is a wondrous sight, very pleasing; and when the consciousness is also attached to this sight that I am the owner of this field and of the pair moving in it, then it truly is a sight that is naturally pleasing.

The desires mentioned here are a minor example of the desires of the self. Some of them are the highest desires in the society to which the Holy Quran was addressing itself at that time, and some are desires which are attractive to the human self in every age. Islam mentions these desires, and determines the worth and value of each, so that these desires remain in their place and do not lay hands on the other values of life.

"Dhalika mata' al-hayat al-dunya" (That is the provision of the life of this world): all these desires that have been presented, or other naturally pleasing things besides them, are the provision for the brief life of this world, and they are not the provision of the exalted and eternal life; nor do they raise a person up to those lofty horizons. These are merely the means of living on this earth nearby. But whoever desires better desires, more precious, higher and purer aims, and wants them so that he does not become absorbed in these earthly desires and worldly lusts, and does not remain lying on the earth instead of rising to the heights, then the one who is truly seeking a lofty nest far above this lowly world, the Holy Quran guides him to that exalted station in this way.

This is the afterlife's provision, which the Quran mentions, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is commanded to give glad tidings about it to the believers who have taqwa. The delights of the Hereafter generally also belong to the realm of human desire, but there is a very great difference between them and worldly rewards and bounties. This is a provision that will be reached only by those who, in this world, were people of taqwa, whose hearts were filled with fear of Allah. Their hearts were full of the remembrance of Allah. The truth is that the awareness of Allah's fear reforms both the spiritual world and the material world at once. It saves the human self from being immersed in base desires, and protects it from becoming lost in those pleasures like animals. People in whose hearts is the fear of God regard even the sensual delights of the next world as elevated above the level of gross physical pleasure. They give it a status higher than mere animal gratification. While living on this earth, they hold in their hearts the desire for that exalted station, before they depart and are taken away from this transient world.

In this pure and complete provision of the next world there is the best recompense for the desires abandoned in this worldly life. Rather, that reward is far greater than those desires. In this world, if they were owners of fields that were green and flourishing and gave good produce, then in the Hereafter they will be given gardens that are complete, beneath which rivers flow, and they will be with the awareness and certainty that they will abide in these gardens forever; and those gardens will also be permanently green, not seasonal. They will not be like the seasonal fields of this world. If in the world there are women and children, there are there very pure spouses; and their purity is, as it were, a distinction and a excellence over worldly spouses. As for choice horses, livestock, fields, and heaps of gold and silver, in this world these resources were means of luxury and a source of supplying desires. In the Resurrection there will be no need for them. Therefore, there will be an abundance of objects of desire there, and they will be obtained in great quantity; so what need of resources when the goal is attained?

And there, beyond the provisions, there will be a great bounty, namely the good pleasure of the Lord of Majesty. This good pleasure is so great a blessing that it outweighs all the desires of this whole world and all the delights of the whole Hereafter. Then reflect on the word ridwan itself: how pleasing the word ridwan is in itself. It is fresh, and carries the fragrance of intimacy and love.

﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of the servants﴾ ……… "and Allah is watchful over His servants." ……… He knows well what the true reality of their nature is, what inclinations are in it, and what guidance this nature needs. He is also aware of these matters. He has sound insight into deciding the affairs of human nature, both in this world and in the Hereafter, because He is the Creator of nature.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 3, verses 16–17:

Here Allah, the Exalted, enumerates the qualities of His special servants: how their relationship with You is, and what deeds make servants deserving of the rewards of the Gardens.

The words that come from their mouths in their supplications are the result of their taqwa (God-consciousness) and fear of Allah. Out of fear of Allah, they first proclaim their faith. Then they make faith their intercessor with Allah, seek forgiveness, and protect themselves from the Fire.

Among all their qualities, one of the highest values of human life is mentioned, and these values are especially important for the Muslim community. They are patient (sabr). In patience, a person bears every grief and sorrow, and whatever hardships come in the way of the Islamic call, he remains steadfast. He fulfils his duties in the path of the Islamic call. He becomes a picture of submission and contentment before Allah, and whatever mountains of calamity the circumstances may bring down upon him, he is content with Allah's decree. They are truthful (sidq), because truth is the foundation of this universe. By holding fast to truth, they rise above ordinary people. The essence of falsehood is that a person abandons truth for some benefit or to avoid some harm.

They are obedient (qunut), thus fulfilling the right of divinity and practising the obligations of servitude on their part, and they worship Allah alone, and no other worship has a place in their conception of life.

The benefit of spending in the way of Allah is that a person is not humiliated by wealth, and he is freed from miserliness. By spending, a person practically gives precedence to human brotherhood over personal desire and pleasure, and creates an atmosphere of collective security that is pleasant for all human beings.

As for seeking forgiveness in the last part of the night, it is a station where there is dense and pleasant shade, whose atmosphere is fresh, and the word "al-asḥār" (the pre-dawn hours) paints a pleasant and tranquil picture of that special time, just before the break of dawn, which is unmatched in its place. It is a time when the universe is extremely calm, the atmosphere is clear, and at that time the spiritual conceptions of the human soul awaken, and good thoughts are inspired upon the mind and heart. When, in this delightful atmosphere, a human being seeks forgiveness in the presence of his Lord, then its reflection also casts very profound spiritual effects upon the human soul. At that time, the soul of the human being and the soul of this universe become aligned and facing in the same direction before the Lord of the universe and the Creator of man.

It is the right of such patient ones, such truthful ones, such obedient ones, such spenders of wealth, and such seekers of forgiveness, that Allah's good pleasure should welcome them, because they are deserving of it. Because the shade of Allah's mercy is dense, and its fruit is fresh, and it has more sweetness than every pleasure and every desire, if one has a sound taste.

Thus the Qur'an, regarding the human being as an earthly creature on this earth, begins guiding the human soul; gradually it elevates it, and takes it to a lofty horizon, to the lights of the exalted assembly, and this process takes place very comfortably, very patiently, with great gentleness and compassion. In this spiritual progress, the nature of the human being and his natural inclinations are fully taken into account. His physical weaknesses and frailties are also kept in mind. Love and its yearning are also stirred. No natural impulse is uprooted, nor is anyone compelled to any action. During this endeavour, ordinary life continues to flow on; no interruption is created in it. This is the fitrah of Allah, this is the system of life of Allah, for this fitrah, and Allah is well aware of the condition of His servants: "wallahu basirun bil-'ibad" (And Allah is All-Seeing of His servants).

* * * * *

Up to this point, the aim of this surah has been to purify the belief in Tawhid, so that Allah is one, He alone sustains this universe, the Messengers who came into the world are also one, and their prophethood is also one unit. It was also explained what the true attitude of the people of faith towards the signs of Allah and the thoughts of Allah should be, and how those whose hearts have crookedness deal with these ideas and verses of the Book. Those who deviate were warned of their evil end, and in this context their attention was drawn to the evil end of deviators from the past and present as an example. After this, it was explained that the belief in Tawhid and the Islamic view of life is a general natural system, and that the natural inclinations are also taken into account in it. But the sight of the God-conscious (muttaqin) rises above these, and they constantly plead before their Lord.

But now, from here until the end of this lesson, we are made acquainted with another reality. This second reality is a necessary consequence of the belief in Tawhid and the Islamic view of life. If the first reality exists, then the second should also exist. That is: the reality of Tawhid should have its embodiment and manifestation in our lives. All these matters are explained in the coming part of this lesson.

The summary of the first part is again impressed upon the mind and kept in view, so that its results may be established through the second reality. This section begins with the testimony that there is no deity except Allah. Angels have also given witness to this belief, and the people of knowledge have also affirmed it. Along with being the Deity, Allah is also al-Qayyum, that is, the Sustainer of this universe, and the meaning of His qayyumiyyah is that He runs this universe and the human being within it according to justice. And when it is established that Allah alone is the Deity and al-Qayyum, then the second matter automatically follows: that people should acknowledge the worship of Allah. This worship should be for Him alone; His command should descend into the life of all human beings; decisions should be made in accordance with it; all servants should bow before Allah in submission; they should bow before Him, obey the Being who is al-Qayyum, and follow the Book He has sent down and the Sunnah of His Messenger.

And the second reality is expressed thus: "Inna'd-din 'indallahi'l-Islam" (Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam). Therefore Allah does not accept any religion other than Islam. And what is Islam? It is to submit, to obey, and to follow in every matter. Therefore the religion accepted by Allah is not merely a rational concept, nor merely belief in the heart; religion is that the demands of this view of life and this affirmation and conviction are also fulfilled, and the demands are that people make decisions in all their affairs according to the Shariah, and then willingly accept whatever the Shariah decides, and obey the Messenger of God in this system.

This is why the Qur'an, in a very striking manner, expresses this reality regarding the People of the Book: they claim to be upon the religion of Allah, but their attitude is that when they are called to the Book of Allah, to decide according to it, a group of them turns away, and thereby the claim of their religion is exposed and it becomes void. The religion accepted by Allah is only Islam, and Islam is not without submitting the head. Islam means obedience to the Messenger of God, and decisions in the affairs of life are made according to the Book of Allah.

Here the cause of turning away and aversion from the Book of Allah has also been mentioned, and it has been described in such a tangible and factual manner that it shows they do not believe in the religion at all, because they do not fully believe in the justice of the Day of Reckoning. They thought that they would remain in the Fire of Hell only for a few days, because they are People of the Book, and in matters of their religion, those beliefs which they had fabricated deceived them. And this was a strange delusion for them. In short, at that time they are neither People of the Book nor People of Religion, nor are they believers. Why? Because when they are called to come and decide some dispute according to their Book, they turn their faces away and flee.

In short, the Qur'an here states the meaning and reality of religion with such certainty and firmness that the religion accepted by Allah for all people is now only the religion of Islam, which is clear, plain and definitive. That is, Islam means deciding in courts according to the Book of Allah, and then accepting it and acting upon it. If someone does not do this, he is not religious; he is not a Muslim, even if he claims religion and claims Islam. The limit of religion that Allah defines, the definition He gives, and the affirmation He makes, is exactly what we have stated above, and Allah, in defining religion, is not subject to anyone's desire; He knows it as it is.

Moreover, whoever takes disbelievers as friends (and the context shows that the disbelievers are those who do not judge according to the Book of Allah in their courts), then he will have no connection with Allah. He will have no relation with Allah in any matter; there will be no link between him and Allah. That is, simply because this person befriended disbelievers, or supported disbelievers, or sought support from disbelievers. And the disbelievers are those who do not decide according to the Book of Allah in their courts, even if they verbally claim that they follow the religion of Allah.

Such strictness is shown in forbidding friendship with disbelievers that, if you do not refrain, your religion will be destroyed at its foundation. Along with this warning and admonition, the Qur'an also explains it well. Muslims are given the insight that Allah alone is the true disposer of all affairs in this entire universe. He is the Sovereign; all matters are in His control. He is the Owner of the Kingdom: He gives kingship to whom He wills and removes it from whom He wills; He honours whom He wills and withdraws honour from whom He wills. And His disposal in the affairs of people's lives is also a part of that cosmic disposal which He exercises to run this universe. Look: He causes the night to enter the day and the day to enter the night; He brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living. And this is His qiyam bil-'adl (upholding in justice), with which He sustains human beings and also sustains the universe. Therefore, what need do the people of faith have to leave Allah and establish friendships with disbelievers, even if the disbelievers' power is very great, their wealth is very great, and their children are very many?

This repeated and emphatic warning and admonition shows that at that time this point had not been clearly explained to the newly formed Muslim community. Some people among the Muslims at that time still maintained their former family, tribal and economic ties. These ties existed simultaneously with the polytheists of Makkah and the Jews of Madinah. Therefore this interpretation of the religion of Islam was given, and they were commanded not to maintain friendly relations with the disbelievers. Also, this verse makes clear that a human being is inclined toward the apparent powers of the world and is influenced by them; therefore they are told who the real power is, what the true reality of those people is, and what the Islamic view of life is, and what its demands are in practical life.

And this lesson concludes with the definitive decision that Islam is the name of obedience to Allah and His Messenger, and that the only way to move toward Allah is to obey the Messenger of Allah. It is not sufficient merely to believe in the testimony of faith with the heart in isolation and to affirm it with the tongue. He says: "Say: If you love Allah, then follow me, and Allah will love you." ……………

"Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger; but if they turn away, then know that Allah does not love the disbelievers." ……………So either there will be following, and if you are fully obedient, Allah will also approve of it; or there will be disbelief, which Allah greatly dislikes. This is the point at which the paths of a Muslim and a disbeliever diverge. This second part of the lesson will now be considered in detail.
